title: Dark Mild Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: Dark mild is a low alcohol, malty English ale with real flavour. Learn its history, numbers and how to taste it.
teaser: Under 4% ABV and still full of chocolate, caramel and toast. Dark mild is the quiet hero of English pubs.
standfirst: Dark mild is one of the lowest alcohol beers in the English tradition and one of the most flavourful for its strength. It packs caramel, toast and a touch of chocolate into a beer of around 3 to 3.8% ABV. Here is how it works.
sections: A light beer that tastes dark

Dark mild is an English ale that looks heavier than it is. It is brown to dark brown, sometimes nearly black, yet usually only around 3 to 3.8% ABV. The BJCP guideline puts its original gravity at roughly 1.030 to 1.038 and its bitterness at around 10 to 25 IBU.

The point of the style is flavour at low strength. A good dark mild gives you caramel, toffee, toast and a little chocolate or dried fruit, with a soft body and a short, clean finish. It is a beer for a long session at the pub, built to be drunk by the pint without leaving you foggy. Our guide to English mild covers the wider family.

In older English brewing, mild meant fresh and unaged. It was the opposite of stale or aged beer, which had been stored for months and picked up sourness. Mild ale was sold young and sweet.

Victorian milds were considerably stronger than today's. Over the twentieth century, wartime restrictions, taxes and changing tastes pushed strength down. By the late twentieth century mild had settled into the low-alcohol beer most drinkers know now. It became the working person's pint in industrial towns, especially in the Midlands, the north-west and Wales.

Mild also became a beer for thirsty workers. Miners, steelworkers and factory hands wanted something that replaced lost fluid after a shift without knocking them over. A low-alcohol, malty, lightly hopped ale fitted that need. The style's modern revival in craft brewing owes something to that history: a beer meant for drinking by the pint, not for showing off.
Where the colour and flavour come from

Dark mild uses a simple pale malt base with crystal malt for caramel sweetness and a small amount of chocolate or black malt for colour and a gentle roast. Some brewers add brown sugar or brewers' caramel. The grist is designed to give maximum flavour from a low gravity wort.

Brewers often mash a little warmer than usual, around 67 to 68 °C, to leave more unfermentable sugars. That keeps the body from feeling watery despite the low alcohol. Hops stay in the background. English varieties such as Fuggle or East Kent Goldings add a little earthy balance, never sharp bitterness.

Traditionally, dark mild is served from the cask. Cask ale is unfiltered, unpasteurised and finishes conditioning in the pub cellar. It is served at cellar temperature, around 11 to 13 °C, with soft, natural carbonation. Those conditions suit dark mild well. Colder, fizzier service hides its delicate malt flavours.

Cask ale is fragile. Once a cask is opened it should be drunk within a few days before it turns stale. That fragility is one reason mild has declined in many places. A low-volume beer in a cask that empties slowly is a hard sell for a busy pub.
Dark mild versus porter and stout

People sometimes confuse dark mild with porter or stout. All three are dark English-tradition beers, but they differ in strength and roast. A dark mild sits around 3 to 3.8% ABV with gentle roast. A porter is usually stronger and more roasty. A stout is roastier still, often with a dry, coffee-like finish.

Think of dark mild as the soft, malty end of the dark beer spectrum. If it tastes sharply roasted or bitter, the brewer has pushed it towards porter. If it tastes thin and watery, the grist did not give enough body for the gravity.
A useful beer for Indian taprooms

Most Indian drinkers know dark beer as strong stout or heavy porter. Dark mild offers something different: full flavour at low strength. In a hot climate that matters. A 3.5% brown beer at 10 to 12 °C can be refreshing in a way that an 8% imperial stout never is.

It pairs well with everyday food too. Try it with keema pav, kathi rolls, roast chicken or a plate of pakoras on a rainy evening. Its caramel and toast flavours meet fried and roasted food comfortably without overwhelming spice.

Light beers are harder to judge than strong ones. There is less alcohol and less sugar to hide behind, so every fault and every bit of thinness shows. Judging whether a dark mild has enough body for its gravity, or whether its roast is clean, is a skill built through guided tasting.

For a first step, pour a dark mild next to a porter. Taste the mild first. Note the body, the roast level and how quickly the flavour fades. Then compare the porter. You will see how much flavour the mild delivers for its strength.
faqs: Usually around 3 to 3.8% ABV, with an original gravity of about 1.030 to 1.038.
In older English brewing, mild meant young and unaged, as opposed to stale or aged beer. It did not originally mean weak.
Is dark mild the same as porter?
No. Dark mild is lower in alcohol and gentler in roast. Porter is usually stronger and more roasty.
How should dark mild be served?
Traditionally from the cask at cellar temperature, around 11 to 13 °C, with soft carbonation.
